'''Mining hardware''' is where the abstract question of what a coin is worth meets a power bill, a purchase order and a shipping date. This page is part of the series under [[How Cryptocurrencies Gain Value]], and it covers the arc from laptop CPUs to the ASIC industry, the '''Butterfly Labs''' era that opened it, why every attempt to build an ASIC-proof coin has eventually failed, and the one piece of real economics underneath all of it — '''cost of production'''.

The reason it belongs in a series about value: proof-of-work is the only part of crypto where somebody must '''spend''' a known amount of real money to produce a coin. That gives a price something nothing else in this field has — a floor made of electricity.

== 1. The four phases ==

The operator of this chain was reading Bitcointalk while this happened, and wrote it down at the time. The account below is his, from the 2020 Steemit post ''Steemit: Under New Management'' and from the project's 2016 CryptoNight analysis; the phrasing in quotes is his.

* '''CPU (2009–2010).''' Ordinary laptops. '''"When it started, you could mine Bitcoin on your laptop, CPU mining, the more Processors your computer had, the better, so you wanted a Quad Core or more. People got thousands of Bitcoin that way."''' This is the only period in Bitcoin's history where the distribution problem described in [[Holders, Rarity, and Distribution]] solved itself, because the means of production was a thing people already owned.
* '''GPU (2010–2012).''' '''"Then some people made Mining software for Gaming Graphics Cards, GPUs."''' Still consumer hardware, bought at a shop, but now you had to '''choose''' to buy it.
* '''ASIC (2013 onward).''' Application-Specific Integrated Circuits, defined plainly: '''"ASICs, which is a whole box of processors running 1 app."''' That is the clearest one-line definition of an ASIC on this wiki. '''"Butterfly Labs was first, then Antminer and others, then it just got crazy with mining farms with warehouses full."'''
* '''The industry.''' What began with Butterfly Labs' first ASICs became, as the Convergence paper puts it, '''an ecosystem of 100-plus mining-rig companies'''. The same observation that paper makes about VR and about cannabis extraction applies here exactly: '''the vision preceded the hardware''', sometimes by decades, and the hardware is what converted the vision into an industry.

== 2. Butterfly Labs, from somebody who was there ==

The firsthand version is two sentences long and contains the whole transition:

> '''"Then there was Butterfly labs, and the mining farms. It no longer became feasible to mine with a laptop or number of laptops, and the Graphics cards that had been being used for mining were also being overtaken by the ASICs."'''

Note what it says: Butterfly Labs did not merely beat laptops, it beat '''the GPUs that had already beaten the laptops'''. Two generations of consumer hardware were retired by one product category, inside about a year.

=== The context it landed in ===

It matters what the community was like when that happened, because the ASIC did not just change the economics — it changed who the project was for. By his account, he arrived via a news story about the Silk Road, saw a '''฿''' symbol being used where a dollar sign should be, pasted it into a search engine and landed on '''Bitcointalk.org''':

* The stated goal then was '''"that everyone would use Cryptocurrency"''' — a decentralised currency not issued as fiat by a government. Early advocacy was door-to-door in the literal sense: '''"We would create email lists of companies and everyone, to tell them about the price rise, and ask them to start accepting Bitcoin for their products."'''
* '''"When I first got there, Bitcoins were $5.00 each. Soon after they were $30.00, then $100.00. Some people said it was a Bubble and it would 'be affordable again.'"''' Everyone traded on '''MtGox''' — an acronym for '''"Magic the Gathering Online Exchange"''' — and '''"you had to use a Money order to buy them."'''
* People were already working out that whole coins would become too valuable to transact in, so the smaller pieces '''"were dubbed 'Satoshis'."'''

That is the world Butterfly Labs shipped into: a forum of people trying to get shops to accept a $5 currency bought by money order. The ASIC arrived and the question stopped being ''how do we get everyone to use this'' and became ''who can afford the hardware''.

=== What the ASIC actually changed ===

Before ASICs, the cost of mining was '''the cost of a computer you already had.''' After, it was a '''capital purchase of single-purpose hardware''' — ordered in advance, manufactured on somebody else's schedule, delivered into a difficulty level that had risen while it was in transit, and worthless for anything else on arrival. That last property is the whole shift. A GPU that stops being profitable gets sold to a gamer. An ASIC that stops being profitable is '''scrap''', and that asymmetry is what turned mining from a hobby into an industry with inventory risk, pre-orders, delivery disputes and balance sheets.

The centralisation that followed was not subtle, and his summary of it is the one to remember: '''"This simply served to make it harder to mine, as more people come in the people with the most power get the most, but it was easier when Laptops were just competing."'''

Three consequences outlived the hardware:

# '''Mining became a business, so it became concentrated.''' Capital, cheap power and wholesale chip access are advantages that compound, and nothing in proof-of-work prevents them from compounding.
# '''The miners became a chokepoint.''' Once production is concentrated, so is the power to decide which transactions enter a block — which is the toll-booth problem in §5 of [[How Cryptocurrencies Gain Value]] and §7 of [[Economics 101 and 102]]. The fee market and the ASIC market are '''the same story at two different layers'''.
# '''Difficulty eats every efficiency gain.''' The protocol adjusts difficulty to hold the block interval, so faster hardware across the network does not produce more coins — it produces '''the same coins for more electricity'''. Individually rational, collectively a treadmill.

=== And the halving pushes the same way ===

Running underneath all of it is the emission schedule, which he states compactly: '''"Blockchain started with 50 Coins per Block that were released, and it halves every few years, so was 25, then 12.5 and may be or is coming up on 6.25. That makes them harder to get and the fees mean more as it gets lower, and they become more rare."'''

That is the link most explanations miss. The halving does two things at once: it makes the coin scarcer, '''and''' it shifts miner income from the block subsidy toward '''fees'''. A chain whose producers are paid less by issuance over time is a chain whose producers care more about the fee auction over time — so the toll booth in §5 of the value page is not a phase, it is the '''designed destination''' of a halving schedule.

== 3. Every ASIC-resistant coin has lost, so far ==

This is the part a project is tempted to skip, and our own corpus does not skip it.

* '''Litecoin''' was built for exactly this reason, and his notes state the motive without decoration: '''"So Litecoin was made, to allow Laptops again, then Feather Coin because Litecoin got ASICs."''' Litecoin and Feathercoin adopted '''scrypt''' on the promise that it resisted Bitcoin's ASICs. The corpus records the outcome plainly: '''scrypt ASICs were developed, and the same centralisation occurred.'''
* '''Dogecoin''' arrived late enough that, as the corpus puts it, '''farms already existed''' by launch. The pattern repeated with no transition period at all.
* '''CryptoNight''' — named after '''kryptonite''', the algorithm being the ASIC's weakness — was the most serious attempt: deliberately memory-hard so that CPUs stayed competitive. Monero was the flagship. The corpus's own retrospective marks it as a '''partial failure''': "Monero eventually faced ASIC pressure, had to fork."
* The community correction recorded alongside that post is the honest footnote: what matters for CryptoNight is '''CPU cache, at least 2MB per core''', not RAM, and many mainstream CPUs did not have it. The conclusion in our own file: '''"more accessible than Bitcoin, but not truly everyman's coin."'''

The general lesson is uncomfortable and worth stating: '''if a hash function is valuable enough to specialise for, somebody will specialise for it.''' ASIC resistance buys years, not permanence.

== 4. Which is why these chains do not mine for consensus ==

The corpus draws the conclusion itself, in 2016, about STEEM: because it is '''Delegated Proof-of-Stake''', there is '''no advantage to ASICs''' — block frequency is identical regardless of hardware. The hardware arms race is not won, it is '''declined'''. [[MELEK Blockchain|MELEK]] inherits exactly that, and it is why MELEK has no mining at all: see [[Proof of Work, Proof of Stake, and DPoS]].

[[PRANA]] does mine, with '''Etchash''', and the distinction is deliberate: PRANA's work is the chain's product rather than only its clock. See [[Proof of Work Mining]] for the algorithms and PRANA's TASK lane. The browser miner on the pool is the same argument as CryptoNight's in a new form — '''put the means of production back on hardware people already own''' — and it carries the same honest caveat: a browser tab cannot compete with a farm, and saying otherwise would be a lie.

== 5. Cost of production — the only floor in crypto ==

Here is the piece that earns this page its place in a series about value.

For a mined coin you can compute what it '''cost''' to make: hash rate, hardware efficiency, electricity price. That figure behaves like a soft floor, for a mechanical reason — when price falls below the cost of production, miners who cannot cover power switch off, hash rate falls, difficulty adjusts down, and supply issuance gets cheaper to produce. Sellers who were selling to pay bills stop existing.

Four honest limits:

* It is a '''soft''' floor. Miners with sunk hardware, subsidised power or a strategic reason will mine at a loss for a long time, and price has traded below estimated production cost in real cycles.
* The floor '''moves''', because difficulty and energy prices move.
* It says nothing about the '''ceiling'''. Cost of production never explains a bull market.
* '''It does not exist for staked chains at all.''' MELEK has no production cost in this sense — its issuance is near-free — so nothing underneath its price comes from physics. That is the trade for being feeless and fast, and it means everything in [[Utilities and Sinks]] has to do the work that electricity does for Bitcoin.

That last bullet is the most useful sentence on this page for anyone holding our coins, which is why it is stated rather than buried.

== Not investment advice ==

This page is hardware history and cost mechanics. It is '''not''' a valuation of any coin, '''not''' a claim that any price has a floor, and '''not''' a suggestion to buy, sell or start mining. Mining is a capital purchase with electricity costs and can lose money.

== Coverage ==
Covers the CPU/GPU/ASIC/industry phases of mining hardware, the Butterfly Labs transition and its three lasting consequences (concentration, the miner chokepoint, the difficulty treadmill), the repeated failure of ASIC resistance across scrypt and CryptoNight, why DPoS declines the arms race while PRANA mines deliberately, and cost of production as a soft price floor that staked chains do not have. '''Sourced from this project's own corpus and the operator's firsthand account rather than from external histories.''' The Butterfly Labs section quotes his 2020 Steemit post ''Steemit: Under New Management'' and his teaching notes directly. Company-level chronology that he did not record — Butterfly Labs' pre-order and delivery disputes and the FTC action against it — is deliberately '''not''' asserted here, because this page's sourcing is the project's own writing.
